<!-- section:hearth-m01-l01-understand -->

Yeasts and bacteria in a starter produce gas and acids at a rate that depends mainly on temperature and food. A recipe that says "ready in four hours" was written for one kitchen. In a cooler room the same starter may need six.

Read the starter instead of the timer. A ripe starter has roughly doubled, shows bubbles through its whole depth, has a slightly domed or just-flattening top, and smells pleasantly sour rather than sharp. Each sign is weak alone; together they are strong evidence.

<!-- section:hearth-m01-l01-example -->

Mira feeds her fictional starter at 8:00 in a 19 °C kitchen. The recipe expects a peak at 12:00. At 12:00 the jar shows a 40% rise and bubbles only near the bottom.

She waits and checks every 45 minutes. At 13:30 the starter has doubled, bubbles run through the jar and the top is just starting to flatten. She mixes the dough then, ninety minutes later than the recipe, and records the room temperature beside the time so her next prediction is better.

<!-- section:hearth-m01-l01-exercise -->

Your starter was fed at 21:00 in a 24 °C room. At 07:00 it has risen and collapsed, leaving streaks on the jar, and it smells sharply of acetone. Decide whether to mix the dough now, and explain what evidence supports your choice.

<!-- section:hearth-m01-l01-solution -->

Do not mix yet. The streaks and collapsed top show the starter peaked hours ago, and the sharp smell suggests the culture is hungry. Feed it again, keep it a little cooler, and mix when it next shows a domed, bubbly peak. The warm room shortened the time to peak; the clock alone would have misled you.

<!-- section:hearth-m01-l01-revisit -->

Come back to this lesson whenever a bake runs early or late. Write down the temperature and the signs you saw, not only the time.
